verses.text: Give ear, you heavens, and I will speak. Let the earth hear the words of my mouth.
My doctrine will drop as the rain. My speech will condense as the dew, as the misty rain on the tender grass, as the showers on the herb.
For I will proclaim Yahweh’s name. Ascribe greatness to our God!
The Rock, his work is perfect, for all his ways are just. A God of faithfulness who does no wrong, just and right is he.
They have dealt corruptly with him. They are not his children, because of their defect. They are a perverse and crooked generation.
Is this the way you repay Yahweh, foolish and unwise people? Isn’t he your father who has bought you? He has made you and established you.
Remember the days of old. Consider the years of many generations. Ask your father, and he will show you; your elders, and they will tell you.
When the Most High gave to the nations their inheritance, when he separated the children of men, he set the bounds of the peoples according to the number of the children of Israel.
For Yahweh’s portion is his people. Jacob is the lot of his inheritance.
He found him in a desert land, in the waste howling wilderness. He surrounded him. He cared for him. He kept him as the apple of his eye.
As an eagle that stirs up her nest, that flutters over her young, he spread abroad his wings, he took them, he bore them on his feathers.
Yahweh alone led him. There was no foreign god with him.
He made him ride on the high places of the earth. He ate the increase of the field. He caused him to suck honey out of the rock, oil out of the flinty rock;
butter from the herd, and milk from the flock, with fat of lambs, rams of the breed of Bashan, and goats, with the finest of the wheat. From the blood of the grape, you drank wine.
But Jeshurun grew fat, and kicked. You have grown fat. You have grown thick. You have become sleek. Then he abandoned God who made him, and rejected the Rock of his salvation.
They moved him to jealousy with strange gods. They provoked him to anger with abominations.
They sacrificed to demons, not God, to gods that they didn’t know, to new gods that came up recently, which your fathers didn’t dread.
Of the Rock who became your father, you are unmindful, and have forgotten God who gave you birth.
Yahweh saw and abhorred, because of the provocation of his sons and his daughters.
He said, “I will hide my face from them. I will see what their end will be; for they are a very perverse generation, children in whom is no faithfulness.

They have moved me to jealousy with that which is not God. They have provoked me to anger with their vanities. I will move them to jealousy with those who are not a people. I will provoke them to anger with a foolish nation.
For a fire is kindled in my anger, that burns to the lowest Sheol,  devours the earth with its increase, and sets the foundations of the mountains on fire.
“I will heap evils on them. I will spend my arrows on them.
They shall be wasted with hunger, and devoured with burning heat and bitter destruction. I will send the teeth of animals on them, with the venom of vipers that glide in the dust.
Outside the sword will bereave, and in the rooms, terror; on both young man and virgin, the nursing infant with the gray-haired man.
I said that I would scatter them afar. I would make their memory to cease from among men;
were it not that I feared the provocation of the enemy, lest their adversaries should judge wrongly, lest they should say, ‘Our hand is exalted, Yahweh has not done all this.’”
For they are a nation void of counsel. There is no understanding in them.
Oh that they were wise, that they understood this, that they would consider their latter end!
How could one chase a thousand, and two put ten thousand to flight, unless their Rock had sold them, and Yahweh had delivered them up?
For their rock is not as our Rock, even our enemies themselves concede.
For their vine is of the vine of Sodom, of the fields of Gomorrah. Their grapes are poison grapes. Their clusters are bitter.
Their wine is the poison of serpents, the cruel venom of asps.
“Isn’t this laid up in store with me, sealed up among my treasures?
Vengeance is mine, and recompense, at the time when their foot slides; for the day of their calamity is at hand. Their doom rushes at them.”
For Yahweh will judge his people, and have compassion on his servants, when he sees that their power is gone; that there is no one remaining, shut up or left at large.
He will say, “Where are their gods, the rock in which they took refuge;
which ate the fat of their sacrifices, and drank the wine of their drink offering? Let them rise up and help you! Let them be your protection.
“See now that I myself am he. There is no god with me. I kill and I make alive. I wound and I heal. There is no one who can deliver out of my hand.
For I lift up my hand to heaven and declare, as I live forever,
if I sharpen my glittering sword, my hand grasps it in judgment; I will take vengeance on my adversaries, and will repay those who hate me.
I will make my arrows drunk with blood. My sword shall devour flesh with the blood of the slain and the captives, from the head of the leaders of the enemy.”
Rejoice, you nations, with his people, for he will avenge the blood of his servants. He will take vengeance on his adversaries, and will make atonement for his land and for his people.
Moses came and spoke all the words of this song in the ears of the people, he and Joshua the son of Nun.
Moses finished reciting all these words to all Israel.
He said to them, “Set your heart to all the words which I testify to you today, which you shall command your children to observe to do, all the words of this law.
For it is no vain thing for you; because it is your life, and through this thing you shall prolong your days in the land, where you go over the Jordan to possess it.”
Yahweh spoke to Moses that same day, saying,
“Go up into this mountain of Abarim, to Mount Nebo, which is in the land of Moab, that is across from Jericho; and see the land of Canaan, which I give to the children of Israel for a possession.
Die on the mountain where you go up, and be gathered to your people, as Aaron your brother died on Mount Hor, and was gathered to his people;
because you trespassed against me among the children of Israel at the waters of Meribah of Kadesh, in the wilderness of Zin; because you didn’t uphold my holiness among the children of Israel.
For you shall see the land from a distance; but you shall not go there into the land which I give the children of Israel.”

footnotes.content: Moses stands at the threshold of his life's end, calling all creation to witness his final testimony. There's a solemnity here—heaven and earth, not just people, must hear what God has done. When we have something true to say, it's worth saying where all can listen.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo in this song: the tender shepherd who calls all creation to witness His covenant, who carries us on eagle wings, who judges sin yet stops Himself for the sake of His name, who promises restoration after judgment. The same God who sang through Moses still keeps covenant with those who turn back to Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: His words come like gentle rain and dew—nourishment, not force. A grandparent's wisdom doesn't shout; it settles quietly on tender grass where it can sink deep and bring life. This is how God speaks through us when we speak truth with humility.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The proclamation of God's name is the center of all Moses says. In Hebrew thought, the name holds the whole character—His faithfulness, power, and covenant. When we speak God's name truthfully, we're not just adding words; we're inviting His presence into the room.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Rock—that's what God is, unchanging and perfect. Moses pivots here from the calling to witness to the reason: God is absolutely trustworthy. Every one of His ways just, every one of His acts right. There's our foundation.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: But the people have done the opposite: they've twisted themselves away. "Not his children because of their defect"—the hurt in these words is real. God is faithful; His people keep choosing crookedness instead. That gap is the whole tragedy of this song.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Moses speaks sharp rebuke now: foolish people who repay their Father's love with ingratitude. He's not just scolding; he's reminding them who they are—purchased, established, claimed. Even the rebuke is an act of belonging.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Ask your father, ask your elders"—this is how Israel stays faithful: by remembering. The generations teach us. Asking our elders isn't weakness; it's the wisdom to know we haven't seen what they've seen, and we need their eyes on history.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God distributed the nations but kept Israel as His own portion. He could have let them drift like all the others, but He numbered them, set them apart. That's the specificity of grace: not general favor for everyone, but a chosen people He'll hold to account.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Yahweh's portion is His people; Jacob is His inheritance. He looks at Israel and sees His own possession, His lot, His treasure. That binding claim is what makes the coming judgment so painful—He loves them fiercely, and their turning away wounds Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: In wilderness and howling waste, God surrounded them, cared for them, kept them as the apple of His eye. That phrase—apple of His eye—is how we speak of what we guard most jealously. Desert or plenty, God's tenderness toward His people never wavered.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: An eagle teaching her young to fly by spreading her wings and letting them ride on her feathers. God's protection is active, not distant—He carries us as we learn. Sometimes He stirs the nest to call us upward; sometimes He bears us on His strength.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Yahweh alone led him. No foreign god, no mixed loyalty. This is the simplicity and power Moses is calling them back to: singular devotion. When we divide our worship, we divide our strength and lose the very protection we're trying to secure.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God made them ride on high places, gave them abundance—honey from the rock, oil from flint. These are real places and real miracles from the journey. The Negev, the wilderness springs: God meets us in the harsh places with exactly what we need.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Butter, milk, fat lambs, finest wheat, wine—the blessing was not spare. God's generous table was set. But here's where the peril begins: abundance without gratitude can turn the heart toward self-sufficiency instead of dependence on the Giver.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jeshurun grew fat and kicked. They were made sleek by God's hand, then used that strength against Him. This is the ancient temptation: mistaking God's provision for our own achievement. The fuller the belly, the easier it is to forget where the bread came from.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They moved Him to jealousy with strange gods. That jealousy isn't petty; it's the pain of abandonment. When someone you've loved and provided for turns to another, the hurt is real. God's jealousy reveals how deep His covenant love actually is.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They sacrificed to demons and new gods their fathers hadn't known. The shock here is that each generation can invent fresh idolatry. It's not always the same false god; it's the constant human creativity in turning away from the true one. We must watch our own hearts for new deceptions.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "You are unmindful of the Rock who became your father." Forgetfulness is at the root. They didn't suddenly hate God; they simply stopped remembering Him. That's how slow the drift is—one day you realize He's not on your mind anymore.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Yahweh saw and abhorred. His heart broke at the sight. The children He'd carried on eagle's wings now provoked Him. There's a rawness in God's grief here—not cold judgment, but the anguish of a parent watching His children trash the inheritance.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "I will hide my face from them." The threat isn't violence but withdrawal. No more presence, no more guidance, no more protection. To a people who've known God's face, His absence is the deepest judgment. Let them see what their end becomes without Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God will provoke them through a foolish nation—make them jealous the way they made Him jealous. It's a mirror: they chose "those who are not a people," so they'll be displaced by them. Judgment sometimes works by turning our choices against us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A fire kindled in God's anger burns to the lowest Sheol. Sheol is the grave, the place beneath all places. This speaks of total devastation, reaching into depths. It's not hyperbole in this context—judgment can be comprehensive and thorough.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "I will heap evils on them. I will spend my arrows on them." The arrows were the tools God used; now they're turned. What was meant for protection becomes the instrument of consequence. God doesn't contradict His nature; He enacts it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Hunger, burning heat, bitter destruction, teeth of wild animals, viper venom—this lists real curses of exile and war. Not poetic flourish but historical consequences: when a people break covenant, they lose the protection that bound them. Nature itself becomes hostile.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Outside the sword bereaves, inside terror. No safety anywhere—not in the streets, not in the home. Young and old alike. This is the totality of judgment: it reaches everyone, spares no one. The covenant people experience the full weight of covenant-breaking.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "I said that I would scatter them afar, make their memory cease." Total erasure—exile so complete they'd be forgotten. But God's next sentence will change everything. He's about to stop Himself. Judgment isn't the last word.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Were it not that I feared the provocation of the enemy"—God stops because of His name's reputation. The enemies would mock Him, claim victory. God's jealousy for His own glory—paradoxically—becomes the reason He doesn't erase His people. He saves them for His name's sake.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The nation is void of counsel, without understanding. Not wicked but foolish—unable to see the pattern of cause and effect. They can't read the story of their own history or foresee their own end. This is the sadness of willful blindness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Oh that they were wise, that they understood this, that they would consider their latter end!" There's a longing in God's voice here—if only they could see the end from the beginning, they'd turn around. But wisdom must be chosen; you can't force someone to be wise.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: How could one chase a thousand if their Rock hadn't sold them? Military logic breaks down: the numbers don't work unless God withdrew protection. One person can't put ten thousand to flight without divine backing. Their defeats announce a spiritual reality.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Their rock is not as our Rock, even our enemies themselves concede." Even the surrounding nations recognized the difference. Israel's defeats proved their God was real—the enemies knew they weren't fighting just flesh and blood. Paradoxically, judgment testifies to God's power.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Their vine is of Sodom, their grapes poison. Sodom and Gomorrah are the byword for destruction. This connects Israel's idolatry to those cities' sins—not just different choices, but the same root corruption. Bad fruit comes from bad roots.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Wine that is serpent poison, asp venom—what looked like nourishment turns deadly. They drank from the cup of false gods believing it was blessing; it was poison. Idolatry doesn't just fail to satisfy; it corrupts from within.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Isn't this laid up in store with me, sealed up among my treasures?" God keeps records. Nothing is forgotten or overlooked. He has their deeds written down, stored in His treasury. That awareness should humble us: all our choices are known and kept.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Vengeance is mine, and recompense." This is the cornerstone verse for justice in Scripture. We don't execute God's judgment; He does. When their foot slides and their calamity comes, it's God's appointed time, not our moment to gloat.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Here's the turn: Yahweh will judge His people—yes—but also have compassion on His servants. When their power is gone and they're utterly broken, that's when mercy arrives. God's judgment isn't the end; it's the threshold to restoration.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Where are their gods, the rock in which they took refuge?" In their humbling, Israel will ask the question they should have asked all along. The empty gods they chose will be exposed as powerless. Reality can't hide when everything is stripped away.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: These gods ate the fat of sacrifices and drank the wine offerings—they were fed well while remaining utterly useless. Israel poured resources into false altars that could never help them. Idolatry isn't just sin; it's wasted love and wasted sacrifice.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "See now that I myself am he. There is no god with me." God declares His absolute sovereignty: He alone kills and makes alive, wounds and heals. No rival exists. No one can pluck Israel from His hand. This is the bedrock truth beneath all judgment and mercy.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God lifts His hand to heaven and swears by His own life. This is the most solemn oath possible—He binds Himself by nothing greater than Himself. What follows is not threat but sacred promise.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: If God sharpens His glittering sword and grasps it in judgment, He will take vengeance on adversaries and repay those who hate Him. The sword shines before it strikes—a warning. God's judgment is not sudden ambush but declared truth that gives time to turn around.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: His arrows will be drunk with blood. It's vivid, terrible language. But notice: the judgment falls on His adversaries and His enemies—those who deliberately oppose Him. God doesn't punish indiscriminately; He judges those who have made themselves His enemies.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Rejoice, you nations, with His people." After all the judgment, the culmination is reconciliation and restoration. Nations are called to rejoice alongside God's people because He has avenged them and made atonement for the land. Judgment leads to peace.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Moses came and spoke all the words of this song in the ears of the people, he and Joshua the son of Nun. The narrative draws back to earth: this isn't just heavenly truth, it's spoken to real people at a real moment. Joshua stands beside Moses—the future leader witnessing the covenant.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Moses finished reciting all these words to all Israel. The song is complete. It's been delivered to the whole assembly. Now they carry these words forward—the choice is theirs.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Set your heart to all the words which I testify to you today." Moses calls for more than hearing—he wants their hearts set. Command your children to observe it, to do it. The covenant lives in the family, passed down. Faithfulness is not private; it's inherited.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "It is no vain thing for you; because it is your life." The Law isn't burden or irrelevance—it's your life itself. Keep it, and you live. The land, the future, your very days depend on covenant faithfulness. God makes the stakes crystal clear.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Yahweh spoke to Moses that same day. Even after the song, God has one more word. It's not judgment on Israel now—it's Moses' own reckoning. The singer must now hear what awaits him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Mount Nebo, the mountain of Abarim across from Jericho—these are real places. Moses will go there and see Canaan. He can look at the promised land but cannot enter it. That sight will be his farewell gift and his final sorrow.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Die on the mountain and be gathered to your people, as Aaron died on Mount Hor. The reference to Aaron makes it clear: this is not an exception but a pattern. Two brothers, two mountains. Moses accepts the same end his brother did.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: You trespassed against me at the waters of Meribah of Kadesh—a specific place, a specific moment. Moses struck the rock in anger instead of speaking to it. He didn't uphold God's holiness before the people. This is why he cannot enter the land: because leaders must honor God's nature even in difficulty.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: You shall see the land from a distance; but you shall not go there. The dream will be visible but unreached. Moses' life ends in longing—faithful service crowned with a sight of the promise he won't inherit. Yet even that sight is grace, not punishment alone. He will know that God kept His word.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
